entries.title: D.C. General Election Guide: What to Know Before Nov. 3
entries.summary: On the heels of a crowded June primary, voters still have plenty left to decide.
entries.content:
On the heels of a crowded June primary, D.C. voters might assume the city’s biggest political decisions are already in the books.

With Democrats holding a decisive registration advantage across the District, nominees Janeese Lewis George for mayor and Robert White for congressional delegate enter the Nov. 3 election as heavy favorites. Yet even frontrunners facing nominal competition say they are taking nothing for granted, routinely reminding supporters that they must still win the general election to secure victory.

The main event is the fight for two available at-large council seats.

That contest will work differently this year thanks to the general-election debut of ranked-choice voting — a structural shift that fundamentally alters how ballots are cast and counted.

Add a citywide measure on restaurant menus to the mix, and D.C. voters still have plenty left to decide.

Here is your guide to what’s on the Nov. 3 ballot, how the new math functions and what you need to know before marking your grid.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

The At-Large Race and the New Math

The pick-two era is officially over. District voters have long been able to make two selections on their ballot for the two open at-large D.C. council seats. Under the city’s new ranked-choice voting system, voters now face a grid prompting them to rank candidates from first to fifth choice.

This shift has created a unique mathematical quirk in the general election.

To determine the two winners, election officials eliminate candidates with the lowest vote totals round by round until two remain. But because each ballot carries only one active vote at a time, a ballot locked on a winning frontrunner stays frozen — meaning your secondary rankings are never used to help select a second winner.

The dynamic stems from the District’s 1973 Home Rule Act, which reserves two of the council’s four at-large seats for non-majority party members. Combining those two seats into a single ranked race means a vote locked on a frontrunner swallows down-ballot influence for the second seat.

In deep-blue Washington, Democratic nominee Oye Owolewa is expected to draw a significant share of first-choice rankings. But Democrats whose votes stay locked with Owolewa effectively surrender their say in deciding which candidate claims the reserved non-majority seat.

That reality has altered traditional campaign strategies.

Independent incumbent Elissa Silverman — who won a June special election to fill the seat vacated by Kenyan McDuffie — has urged her supporters to rank her number one, explicitly warning that ranking a Democrat first impacts her chances.

Owolewa is countering by asking Democrats to lock in his victory as their top pick. Meanwhile, Republican Darrell Green and Statehood Green candidate Darryl Moch are competing for those same top-tier rankings in hopes of pulling off an upset.

Confusion caused by this change has been compounded by delays in voter education materials from the D.C. Board of Elections, which told The Washington Sun it faced procurement delays at the start of the fiscal year.

Janeese Lewis George (7619x5080, AR: 1.50)
The Top of the Ticket

Other races on the general election ballot follow more traditional dynamics. In the mayoral contest, Lewis George is heavily favored to succeed retiring Mayor Muriel Bowser. She faces Independent Rhonda Hamilton and Statehood Green candidate Robert L. Gross.

In the race to succeed Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton as D.C.’s nonvoting voice in Congress, White faces Republican Denise Rosado and Statehood Green candidate Kymone Freeman.

Further down the ballot, two Democratic incumbents in citywide seats are seeking another term: Council Chairman Phil Mendelson faces Republican challenger Abi-Ananiah Prudent, while Attorney General Brian Schwalb defends his seat against Republican Manuel Rivera.

In the ward-level council races, three Democratic incumbents are defending their seats alongside one open-seat race:

  • Ward 1: Democratic nominee Aparna Raj faces Republican Jett James Jasper, independent Ryan Prince and Statehood Green candidate Jude Crannitch. 
  • Ward 3: Incumbent Matthew Frumin is running unopposed. 
  • Ward 5: Incumbent Zachary Parker faces Republican Jeffrey Kihien-Palza and Statehood Green candidate Joyce Robinson-Paul. 
  • Ward 6: Three-term incumbent Charles Allen faces Republican Jorge Rice
Voters will also weigh in on the city’s nonvoting shadow U.S. senator and representative seats, as well as several distinct ward-level seats on the State Board of Education.

A Ballot Measure on Foie Gras

Voters will also decide on Initiative No. 86, officially titled the Prohibiting Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026. A “yes” vote supports banning the force-feeding of poultry to produce foie gras and prohibits sale or distribution of those products in the District.

How and When to Vote 

Ballots were mailed to all registered D.C. voters in late September. You can return yours by mail — as long as it is postmarked by Election Day — or drop it into one of the city’s secure 24/7 ballot drop boxes.

  • Early Voting: Runs daily from Monday, Oct. 26 through Sunday, Nov. 1 between 8:30 a.m. and 7 p.m.
  • Election Day: Vote centers are open Tuesday, Nov. 3 from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m.
  • Same-Day Registration: Available at any early voting center or Election Day polling place with proof of D.C. residence. 
Polling locations and drop box sites can be found on the D.C. Board of Elections website.

entries.title: Ukrainian Defense Tech Companies Pitch U.S. Partnerships Despite Political Turmoil
entries.summary: As relations between the countries hit another rough patch, the firms say they can be the bridge while helping both militaries evolve.
entries.content:
Despite freshly strained relations between President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukrainian defense tech companies are courting partnerships with U.S. manufacturers, investors and the Pentagon. The firms are betting that their battlefield-tested weapons could help shore up the countries’ shaky security partnership.

“The deeper we have integration of the industries, the better we are on the political level,” said Roman Tkachenko, co-founder of Tencore, a Ukrainian manufacturer of uncrewed ground vehicles.

Tkachenko was among representatives of 17 Ukrainian defense technology companies exhibiting quadcopters of various sizes, signal jammers and uncrewed ground vehicles at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual conference in Washington last week. It was the conference’s first dedicated Ukraine pavilion.

The push reflects Ukraine’s growing ambitions to become a supplier of military technology rather than simply a recipient of American aid. Kyiv has eased weapons export restrictions, sought joint drone production with the U.S. and discussed a deal in which the Pentagon would purchase Ukrainian-made drones that the two countries would co-produce.

But the relationship hit another rough patch in recent days.

Trump announced a proposed deal this month to import Russian diesel, potentially providing billions of dollars to Russia’s economy. He also demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries, strikes that have damaged Moscow’s energy industry and become an important part of Kyiv’s war effort.

Trump subsequently announced an energy ceasefire, but neither Russia nor Ukraine confirmed agreeing to the terms, and Russia continued attacking Ukraine’s infrastructure.

The tensions deepened Wednesday when Ukraine discovered new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink satellite terminals, prompting Ukrainian officials to suspect that Trump had ordered the limitations.

John Roberts, an American advising Ukraine’s Third Army Corps, said the uncertainty surrounding U.S. military supplies has forced Ukrainian commanders to scramble their battlefield plans.

“We have to fight with what we have, and sometimes we’re told we don’t have as much stuff coming next week,” Roberts said. “When we do our forecast, it means we have to change operations.”

That’s also made Ukraine more determined to reduce its dependence on foreign military aid, Roberts said.

“Ukrainians want to be self-sufficient,” he said.

Tkachenko’s company is seeking American manufacturing partners after establishing a joint venture with Germany’s Quantum Systems and another partnership in Finland. Tencore plans to produce 2,000 ground vehicles through the German partnership over the coming year.

“I cannot tell the politicians what to do,” Tkachenko said. “But what I can do — actually, I can do my job, and I hope that my job will help to make the connection between the countries stronger.”

Tkachenko said nearly 6,000 of his company’s uncrewed ground vehicles have been deployed along Ukraine’s front lines, transporting ammunition and supplies through areas too risky to send soldiers.

Tencore has repeatedly updated its vehicles based on feedback from those troops, the type of rapid adaptation the Pentagon says it wants to achieve.

American manufacturers remain years away from matching Ukraine's drone production, which is expected to reach 6 million to 7 million small attack drones this year.

The Pentagon is seeking to rapidly fill that gap through its $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program, which has already attracted Ukrainian manufacturers. The program ordered 2,000 drones from Ukrainian Defense Drones, the American partner of Ukrainian manufacturer F-Drones.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has also announced plans for a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command and is pressing Congress to approve $50 billion for drones as part of a broader $350 billion defense spending package.

But converting Ukraine’s battlefield-tested weapons into products the Pentagon can buy is a challenge. Federal restrictions on the U.S. military’s use of Chinese-made drones and components — enshrined in the National Defense Authorization Act — complicate Ukrainian manufacturers’ efforts to enter the American market because many rely heavily on Chinese suppliers.

“We've learned a lot from Ukraine, but you can't use everything that's in Ukraine because of all the Chinese components involved in it,” Hegseth said on stage at the AUSA conference.

Ukrainian manufacturers at the conference told The Washington Sun that they are developing versions of their weapons that meet American requirements, though replacing Chinese parts could make them more expensive and harder to produce at scale.

David Hensley, co-founder of Fenicks Group, the American company that organized AUSA’s Ukraine pavilion, said the companies his firm represents offer export models without Chinese components.

“They're all NDAA compliant,” Hensley said, adding that Ukrainian weapons are still cheaper than American products, despite the cost of replacing Chinese parts.

Bohdan Shtylyk, head of exports at Ukrainian drone manufacturer Stellarion, said eliminating Chinese components is possible but difficult because alternative suppliers cannot always meet the industry's production needs.

“Not every factory can match that pace,” Shtylyk said.

He said Stellarion, which produces tens of thousands of drones each month, is investing heavily in versions designed to meet U.S. requirements.

Meta Bureau, another Ukrainian company, is preparing to compete for Pentagon business with a version of its SkyKnight reusable bomber drone that replaces Chinese-made components with alternatives that meet American requirements.

Yuri Hundych, the company’s chief commercial officer, said American companies at AUSA offered the company motors, software and other technologies for its drones.

The company was invited to enter SkyKnight in a Defense Department competition next month at Michigan’s Camp Grayling, where manufacturers will demonstrate systems for possible U.S. military purchase.

Ukraine, he predicted, will remain dependent on Chinese parts as long as they are cheaper. But he said he hopes allies can expand non-Chinese supply chains enough that alternative parts are comparably priced.

“Our conflict is going into its fifth year, and budgets are limited,” he said. “You need to count every penny and give our army and our soldiers these solutions as cheaply as possible and still try to [maintain] a high level of quality.”

Still, Maj. Gen. Duane Miller, a former deputy commanding general of Security Assistance Group-Ukraine, said the Pentagon has a lot to learn from the close relationships between Ukrainian companies that make weapons and the troops that use them.

That relationship allows Ukrainian manufacturers to regularly update their equipment based on battlefield experience, he said, comparing it to commercial smartphone software. By contrast, he said, the U.S. military has traditionally bought equipment, trained soldiers to use it and moved on.

“You can’t make changes in weeks and months. You’re going to have to do this in hours and days,” he said. “The enemy is constantly adapting. What I fear is that we’re not going to learn quickly enough.”

entries.title: All-DMV High School Football Players of Week 8
entries.summary: This weekend’s standouts include a specialist from Friendship Collegiate and a hard-hitting safety from C.H. Flowers.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

This group of high school football standouts got the job done on offense, defense and special teams. Here are five players who excelled in Week 8:

King Antoine, Junior, Linebacker, St. John’s

Antoine shined on defense for the Cadets, who allowed just seven points in a 38-7 win over Good Counsel on Friday in Olney. With the junior linebacker leading the charge, St. John’s nabbed three pick-sixes on a rainy night. Antoine also contributed on offense, coming in to spell senior Da’Jon Talley-Rhodes at running back late in the second half and muscling his way through several Falcons defenders for an impressive rushing score.

“He made big plays for us on both sides of the ball,” coach Terrence Byrd said. “He was a major spark for the team.”

Jedidiah Cook, Senior, Athlete, Friendship Collegiate

Cook made his mark on special teams for the Knights, who earned a dominant victory over KIPP. Cook took the opening kickoff 96 yards for a touchdown to give Friendship Collegiate an immediate jolt in what would be a 54-0 win.

Later in the game, Cook fielded a Panthers punt and sprinted to his right. With no opening in sight, he bounced back left, found a crease and took off for another impressive touchdown. The senior had another long punt return ruled down at the 1-yard line.

Cavare Durandisse, Junior, Athlete, C.H. Flowers

The Jaguars leaned heavily on their defense in a Saturday afternoon slugfest against Prince George’s County rival Oxon Hill. Flowers produced a late defensive stand and held the Clippers to just 12 points in a 14-12 victory. Flowers is now 5-1 under first-year coach Frederick Groves.

Durandisse picked up six solo tackles at safety, including several hard hits that created incompletions. The do-it-all junior, who also plays both running back and slot receiver for the Jaguars, accumulated 126 all-purpose yards and a touchdown on offense.

Collin Henriques, Junior, Wide Receiver, Oakton

Henriques couldn’t be stopped Friday against Westfield. The junior wide receiver scored a touchdown nearly every time he touched the ball in a 35-20 win against the Bulldogs. Henriques pulled in five catches for 180 yards and four touchdowns at wide receiver and added 80 kick return yards on special teams.

With the win, Oakton moved to 7-0 for the first time since 2011 and clinched a Virginia Class 6 playoff berth. The win also snapped the program’s 14-year drought against Westfield.

Caleb Smallwood, Junior, Running Back, Magruder

Smallwood ran for 295 yards and three touchdowns for the Colonels, who needed every yard from their bell-cow back in a thrilling comeback victory over Kennedy on Thursday. In a 50-38 win, Magruder scored 22 points in the fourth quarter. Smallwood also played defense in the second half — he forced and recovered a fumble late in the fourth quarter to help seal the victory.

Between Smallwood and junior Nico Gilliam, the Colonels ran for 400-plus yards and six touchdowns on the evening.

“When we saw on film that Kennedy really liked to blitz, and our offense is a zone RPO scheme, we told our offensive line that they’re going to be bringing six to eight guys every single play,” Magruder coach Ray Fowle said. “Every single play, every single gap, win your assignment. … We've got two guys that can go to the house.”
